When the system becomes surcharged during periods of high runoff, it is so designed to dump the excess effluent into the Susquehanna River through a system of overflow basins located along the Front Street Interceptor - a 30" x 36" concrete pipe located in the bank area of River Front Park (see appendix E). At present, the City is under a mandate from the State Department of Environmental Resources to upgrade the treatment facility; however, the separation of the combination storm and sewage systems is not comtemplated by the City at this time. Since the treatment facility is presently adequate to handle the situation under normal conditions, no moratorium on new sewer service expansion has been imposed by the State for the the areas serviced by the plant.
Many of the sewers within the project area (see Existing Public Utilities Map, appendix E) are of the combination type described above, storm and sanitary. Several of the basins subject to overflowing are located within the project area and vent into the River from their locations in River Front Park. The sewers within the project, as in other parts of Harrisburg, have been in operation for many years. Some of the project sewers leading to the Front Street Interceptor were constructed in the late eighteen hundreds (some as early as 1879). The Geiger Street sewer, a typical project sewer, was constructed in 1895. Unlike many of the earlier sewers in the project which were built with a double ring of brick, it is constructed of 18" terracotta pipe. These older terra-cotta and brick sewers held up under the storm and flooding. Subsidence in the street area around some sewers did occur. A number of the project sewers became clogged during the Storm with debris, but have subsequently been cleared by the City.
During the 1972 Flood, considerable basement flooding occurred due to the backup of the combined sewage system throughout Harrisburg and in the project as well. Unable to discharge the enormous volumes of local runoff into already swollen streams, the surcharged storm sewers caused considerable flooding even before streams had overflowed their banks. In addition, the combined sewage regulators malfunctioned, and allowed the sanitary sewers to become surcharged with resultant popping of manhole covers and excessive loading of sewage lift stations and interceptors. To what extent this action has depreciated the project sewers is not known.
